children: During his keynote address at Nvidia's GTC Berlin conference on Wednesday CEO Jensen Huang claimed the company's new, modular, containerized DSX Pod will bring data center server installation time from "four to five months down to about a month."

This compressed time to first use attacks an issue for Nvidia's customers, especially the public ones that have to report earnings every quarter. Companies are sending their capital expenditures down a black hole for more than a quarter before those assets can begin producing revenue. Everyone can see the equipment Capex and the mounting depreciation expenses, but the revenue will not come for another quarter or two.

This has become such an issue that some Nvidia customers have begun to try to explain the effects of this lag on quarterly earnings. "We incur lease and power costs while depreciating server and other data center equipment during the fit-out process," said CoreWeave chief financial officer Nitin Agrawal on the company's February first-quarter earnings call. "During that period, we recognize costs, but no revenue, causing these new deployments to run at negative contribution margins."
CoreWeave has also included a slide in its quarterly presentation deck that adds more detail to the timing of expenses and revenue.

The point of the DSX Pod is to shorten that period in which expenses are booked, but there is no revenue. For very large data centers, this can be billions of dollars in sales that are pushed forward by a quarter or more.

"The more successful you are, the more people want a chunk of your business and then another chunk and then another until there is nothing left," wrote former Intel CEO Andy Grove in his legendary book, Only the Paranoid Survive. "I believe that the prime responsibility of a manager is to guard constantly against other people's attacks and to inculcate this guardian attitude in the people under his or her management."
Huang has taken this message to heart, and is fighting off the competition with a blizzard of innovation.

When the artificial-intelligence boom began at the end of 2022, Nvidia had already been preparing for it for 15 years. Huang had envisioned a world in which the company's graphics processing units would do much more than just drive computer monitors. By 2022, its data center GPUs were already outselling its gaming line, and this year analysts expect the segment to produce $382 billion in revenue.

Despite all its biggest customers desperately seeking a more varied supply chain for AI computing hardware, Nvidia remains the leader four years later because it has not rested on past accomplishments and has rapidly evolved its AI server platform, resulting in even more Nvidia-designed chips and software going into each server.

Nvidia has even revolutionized the form factor for servers. In 2022, a typical AI server had eight Nvidia GPUs and two Intel CPUs. Four of those servers fit into a standard data-center rack, which contained 32 GPUs in all.

Then in 2024, Nvidia introduced the NVL72 server design where the entire rack was a single server with 72 GPUs and 36 Nvidia CPUs. This has the effect of increasing the amount of data a single server could process at once. It also shortened installation and integration time when building data centers by moving tasks from construction to assembly.

Now Nvidia wants to increase that second benefit by putting seven integrated NVL72 racks into a shipping container-504 GPUs in one modular package-for the new DSX Pod reference design. They will begin shipping in early 2027. The containers will be ready to deploy at a prepared data center site, and just need hookups to the facility's electricity, water and heat-rejection infrastructure.
Building data centers has traditionally been a slow process. Anything Nvidia can do to speed it up will likely be good for its customers' bottom lines, and keep alternatives less attractive.
